abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a unified mathematical framework for understanding neural computation in biological neural networks through the lens of information-theoretic principles. Traditional models of neural networks have predominantly relied on rate-based coding assumptions, which fail to capture the temporal dynamics essential to real neural processing. We propose a novel paradigm shift by formulating neural computation as a dynamic Bayesian inference process operating on sparse spike trains. Our framework treats cortical columns as hierarchical generative models that perform probabilistic inference through message passing on recurrently connected networks. We derive conditions under which spike-timing dependent plasticity naturally implements variational learning in this framework, establishing rigorous connections between synaptic plasticity rules and the minimization of free energy. Analytical results demonstrate that this approach provides a unified explanation for diverse experimental phenomena, including sensory cortex plasticity, attention modulation, and working memory maintenance. The theoretical contributions include novel proofs showing that temporal coding enables exponentially more efficient representation than rate coding for certain computational problems. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for understanding how neural circuits implement probabilistic computation through spike-based dynamics, offering fresh perspectives on the computational architecture of biological intelligence.

We present a rigorous theoretical analysis that significantly advances the mathematical foundations of gradient-based learning in recurrent neural networks. While prior theoretical work has established conditions for convergence in echo state networks and related reservoir computing paradigms, fundamental questions regarding representational capacity and learning dynamics remain unresolved. This paper derives novel bounds on the memory capacity of linear recurrent networks under realistic constraints, substantially improving upon classical results by incorporating finite precision effects and biologically plausible Dale's law constraints. We prove that carefully structured recurrent connectivity enables linear networks to store and retrieve sequential information with capacity scaling logarithmically with network size, resolving an open problem in the field. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to nonlinear recurrent networks by establishing new conditions under which approximation guarantees hold for dynamical systems modeling. Our theoretical framework provides precise characterizations of the eigenvalue spectra necessary for stable memory retention, yielding improved design principles for reservoir computers. Numerical experiments on benchmark sequence processing tasks validate our analytical predictions, demonstrating that networks designed according to our derived criteria achieve superior performance compared to existing approaches. This work bridges the gap between abstract dynamical systems theory and practical network design.

We introduce MetaPlasticity Networks (MPNs), a novel computational architecture that fundamentally reimagines how artificial systems can exhibit adaptive learning through meta-learned plasticity rules. Unlike conventional neural networks that employ fixed or heuristically designed learning rules, MPNs learn their own plastic updating mechanisms through a bilevel optimization process operating over multiple timescales. The system architecture comprises a primary network performing the target computation and a companion meta-network that generates plasticity coefficients based on ongoing network dynamics. This design enables the system to dynamically modulate its own learning rate, selective attention, and synaptic consolidation in response to task demands. We demonstrate that MPNs exhibit remarkable capabilities including continuous learning without catastrophic forgetting, rapid adaptation to novel task domains, and emergent curriculum learning. The architecture incorporates biologically motivated mechanisms including eligibility traces, neuromodulatory gating, and homeostatic regulation. Extensive evaluation across few-shot learning benchmarks, continual learning scenarios, and transfer learning tasks demonstrates that MPNs substantially outperform existing meta-learning approaches while requiring fewer parameters. Analysis of learned plasticity rules reveals interpretable structures resembling attention-like modulation and novelty-gated consolidation. This work establishes a new paradigm for designing adaptive neural systems that continuously evolve their learning mechanisms.

We present an enhanced spiking neural network architecture that achieves substantial improvements in computational efficiency and pattern recognition accuracy through novel integration of temporal dynamics and attention mechanisms. While existing spiking network models demonstrate promising energy efficiency, they typically struggle to match the performance of artificial neural networks on complex pattern recognition tasks. Our system introduces Hierarchical Temporal Spiking Attention (HTSA), which combines sparse coding in spiking neurons with a learned attention mechanism that dynamically routes information through pathway-selective subnetworks. The network operates through precisely timed spikes that encode both rate and temporal information, enabling efficient representation of complex input patterns. We design a biologically plausible training algorithm combining surrogate gradient descent with Hebbian plasticity rules for the attention pathway, eliminating the need for exact gradient computation while maintaining training stability. Implementation on neuromorphic hardware demonstrates that HTSA achieves 94.7% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 78.3% on ImageNet while consuming 12 times less energy than comparable deep networks. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component contributes meaningfully to overall performance. The system exhibits graceful degradation under noise and demonstrates robust transfer learning capabilities. This work significantly advances the state-of-the-art in efficient neuromorphic computing for visual pattern recognition.
